y-m-69-01.title: Where did Minjae's parabola solution go wrong?
y-m-69-01.topic: Focus and directrix of a parabola
y-m-69-01.goal: Find the line in a solution for the focus and directrix of a parabola where the position of the directrix goes wrong, check it using the definition (the distances to the focus and to the directrix are equal), and build a point on the same parabola yourself.
y-m-69-01.material: Minjae found the focus and directrix of the parabola y²=−8x (read: y squared equals minus 8 x). On the coordinate plane the x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis is vertical. Look at whether each line of the solution follows correctly from the line before it.
y-m-69-01.thinking.0: Locate the error in the solution
y-m-69-01.thinking.1: Choose ways to check the result using the definition
y-m-69-01.thinking.2: Build a point that satisfies the conditions yourself
y-m-69-01.prereq.0: You learned a parabola as 'the set of points that are the same distance from one point (the focus) and one line (the directrix)'.
y-m-69-01.prereq.1: Experience working with equations of the form y²=4px (including the fact that the direction it opens depends on the sign of p)
y-m-69-01.prereq.2: Distance between two points on the coordinate plane, and distance from a point to a vertical line
y-m-69-01.prereq.3: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in this solution that you cannot trust. (You may choose the line where the error first appears, or a line where a wrong value shows up because of that error.)
y-m-69-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check, one line at a time, whether each line follows legitimately from the line right before it.
y-m-69-01.s.s1.hint.1: For the point (−2, 4) on the curve, find the distance to the focus and the distance to the directrix Minjae wrote, and compare them.
y-m-69-01.s.s1.line.0: y²=−8x has the form y²=4px, so 4p=−8 and p=−2.
y-m-69-01.s.s1.line.2: The directrix is x=p, that is, x=−2.
y-m-69-01.s.s1.line.3: The point (−2, 4) is on the curve: 4²=16 and −8×(−2)=16.
y-m-69-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 went wrong. The directrix is on the opposite side of the vertex from the focus, so if the focus is (−2, 0), the directrix is x=2. Lines 1, 2 and 4 are correct calculations. The point (−2, 4) in line 4 really is on the curve. But the distance from this point to the focus (−2, 0) is 4, and the distance to Minjae's directrix x=−2 is 0, which does not match the definition. Going back over the result with a point on the curve like this reveals the error.
y-m-69-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the checks that could reveal the error in the directrix of Minjae's solution.
y-m-69-01.s.s2.hint.0: If the solution is wrong, think about which fact it contradicts. What is the definition of a parabola?
y-m-69-01.s.s2.hint.1: Think one by one about whether each check gives information about the 'position of the directrix'.
y-m-69-01.s.s2.o.a: Redo the calculation of p from 4p=−8 from the beginning
y-m-69-01.s.s2.r.a: Repeating only the calculation gives the same value. This misses that the error is in 'interpreting the value (the position of the directrix)'.
y-m-69-01.s.s2.o.b: Compare, for one point on the curve, the distance to the focus and the distance to the directrix
y-m-69-01.s.s2.r.b: This is a check that goes back over the result using the definition. This choice shows you understand the parabola from its definition.
y-m-69-01.s.s2.o.c: Substitute the point (−2, 4) into the equation to check whether it is on the curve
y-m-69-01.s.s2.r.c: This only confirms that the point is on the curve; it cannot tell you whether the positions of the focus and directrix are right.
y-m-69-01.s.s2.o.d: Look at which way the curve opens and decide which side the directrix should be on
y-m-69-01.s.s2.r.d: This is a check of position using a picture or the opening direction. This choice means you remembered that the directrix is on the side opposite to the way the curve opens.
y-m-69-01.s.s2.o.e: Check again that the coordinates of the focus lie on the x-axis
y-m-69-01.s.s2.r.e: It is already correct that the focus is on the x-axis. Rechecking a correct line does not reveal the error.
y-m-69-01.s.s2.explain: Going back over a point on the curve using the definition (the distances to the focus and to the directrix are equal), and checking which side the directrix is on from the opening direction, both reveal the error. Checks that only repeat the calculation or only recheck true facts cannot catch the wrongly interpreted line.
y-m-69-01.s.s3.prompt: Consider the parabola y²=8x, whose directrix is x=−2. Among the points P(x, y) on the curve, make 3 points where both x and y are positive integers, with different values of x.
y-m-69-01.s.s3.hint.0: For y to be an integer in y²=8x, think about what kind of number 8x must be.
y-m-69-01.s.s3.hint.1: Try small values of x in turn and find the cases where 8x is a perfect square.
y-m-69-01.s.s3.ok.c1: x and y are positive integers.
y-m-69-01.s.s3.fail.c1: x and y must both be positive integers.
y-m-69-01.s.s3.ok.c2: The point is on the curve y²=8x.
y-m-69-01.s.s3.fail.c2: The square of y is not equal to 8x. The point is not on the curve.
y-m-69-01.s.s3.explain: For example, (2, 4), (8, 8) and (18, 12). These points have the form x=2k² and y=4k. Their distances to the focus (2, 0) are 4, 10 and 20, and the distances to the directrix x=−2 are the same, so they match the definition. You can also see that the distance is easy to find as x+2.

y-m-69-02.title: A curve drawn with a string and two pegs
y-m-69-02.topic: Definition of an ellipse (the sum of distances from two points)
y-m-69-02.goal: For a curve drawn with two pegs and a string, revise your guesses as information is given one piece at a time, decide what shape the condition 'the sum of the distances is constant' makes, including the case where no curve can be drawn, and build points that fit the condition yourself.
y-m-69-02.material: A gardener drives two pegs into the ground 6 m apart (F and F′) and ties the two ends of a 10 m string to the pegs. Pulling the string taut with the tip of a stick, the gardener goes all the way around to draw a curve. Call the point at the tip of the stick P. The string is then split into two parts, PF and PF′, and the lengths of the two parts always add up to 10 m. Let O be the midpoint of segment FF′.
y-m-69-02.thinking.0: Revise your guess with information given step by step
y-m-69-02.thinking.1: Test the condition with extreme cases
y-m-69-02.thinking.2: Build points that fit the condition yourself
y-m-69-02.prereq.0: Distance between two points and the Pythagorean theorem
y-m-69-02.prereq.1: How to find the coordinates of points and distances on the coordinate plane
y-m-69-02.prereq.2: Having been introduced to an ellipse as 'the set of points whose distances from two points add up to a constant' (even if you have not, you can follow this task from its explanations)
y-m-69-02.prereq.3: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose a guess using only what you know now, and check how your guess changes in light of the revealed information.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, tell apart whether the newly learned information narrows the range of the length or fixes its value.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the length of the string with the distance between the pegs and think about the condition under which a curve forms.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.0.info: The pegs are 6 m apart and the string is 10 m. Place segment FF′ along the horizontal axis, and let h be the distance from O to the farthest point the curve reaches in the direction perpendicular to segment FF′ (upward).
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: Guess h using only what you know now.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.0.after: You cannot know the exact value yet; you can only give a range. If the tip of the stick is right above O and both parts of the string have the same length, each part is 5 m, so h has to be shorter than 5 m.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You decided by only comparing with 3 m, half the distance between the pegs. You have not yet considered how the 10 m length of the string affects h.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: h is at least 3 m and at most about 5 m
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You guessed the range by using the fact that the string is split into two parts.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You may not have connected the fact that the whole string is 10 m to each part being about 5 m.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The exact value cannot be known yet
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a careful judgment: you do not claim an exact value and wait for more information.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.1.info: The highest point T of the curve is right above O. Since T is symmetric left and right, TF=TF′, and the two parts add up to 10 m, so each is 5 m. Also OF=3 m.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, how much is h (the height from O to T)?
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.1.after: In triangle OFT, OF=3, FT=5, and the right angle is at O. So h=√(5²−3²)=4 m. Your first-step guess of at most 5 m was right, and now the value is fixed.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You read the length of one part of the string directly as the height. That part lies at a slant.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You simply subtracted 3 m from 5 m. You did not draw which sides of a right triangle the three lengths are.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You used the fact that the three points O, F and T form a right triangle.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Cannot be known because information is missing
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You may have missed that the symmetry information fixes the length.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Change the string to 6 m and draw in the same way. The string length is equal to the 6 m distance between the pegs.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What shape does the curve drawn by the tip of the stick have?
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.2.after: If P is on segment FF′, then PF+PF′=6, but at points off the segment, PF+PF′ is greater than 6. So when the string is 6 m, segment FF′ itself is the whole curve. An ellipse appears only when the string is longer than 6 m.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: A very flat ellipse is drawn
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You continued the trend that the shape gets flatter as the string gets shorter. You did not consider whether the shape 'ellipse' itself is kept at the end.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It is drawn only on segment FF′
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You used the fact that PF+PF′ cannot be less than FF′.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You thought the curve gets smaller as the string gets shorter. You missed that the pegs are apart from each other.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You mixed up a curve whose points are all the same distance from one point (a circle) with a curve where the sum of distances from two points is constant.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.info: This time, change the string to 5 m. The distance between the pegs stays 6 m.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.ask: Can a curve be drawn with the stick?
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.after: For any point P, PF+PF′ must be at least FF′=6 (the sum of two sides is at least the third side). If the string is 5 m, you cannot even pull it taut with its two ends tied to the pegs, so no curve is drawn.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.r.a: You simply continued the trend that the curve gets smaller as the string gets shorter.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.o.b: The string is too short to pull taut
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.r.b: You noticed that the string cannot cover the 6 m distance between the two pegs.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.o.c: Only part of segment FF′ is drawn
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You applied the shape that appeared with the 6 m string directly to the 5 m string.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.o.d: It depends on where the string is knotted
y-m-69-02.s.s1.st.3.r.d: You focused on another condition of the string rather than the fact that the string cannot span the gap between the pegs.
y-m-69-02.s.s1.reflect: An ellipse could be drawn only when the string length (the sum of distances) is greater than the distance between the pegs; when equal it was a segment, and when smaller it could not be drawn. As information increased, your first 'range guess' was right, but the value was fixed only after using symmetry and a right triangle. Say where your guess changed and where it stayed the same.
y-m-69-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one P first, find its distance to each peg, and check the sum.
y-m-69-02.s.s2.hint.1: After fixing x, change y little by little and find where the sum of the distances becomes 10.
y-m-69-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the distances to the two pegs is 10.
y-m-69-02.s.s2.explain: For example, (0, 4), (3, 3.2) and (4, 2.4). At (0, 4) the distances to the pegs are 5 and 5; at (3, 3.2) they are 3.2 and 6.8; at (4, 2.4) they are 2.6 and 7.4, so the sums are all 10. (−3, 3.2) is a point of the same kind, symmetric to (3, 3.2) left and right.

y-m-69-03.title: If we only give the asymptotes, is the hyperbola determined?
y-m-69-03.topic: Asymptotes of a hyperbola and determining its equation
y-m-69-03.goal: Confirm that there are many hyperbolas with the same asymptotes, decide what extra information that sets the size is needed to pin down a single hyperbola, and build equations that fit the conditions yourself.
y-m-69-03.material: There is a hyperbola x²/a²−y²/b²=1 (read: x squared over a squared minus y squared over b squared equals 1; a>0, b>0) with center at the origin and main axis (the axis joining the two vertices) along the x-axis. The two asymptotes of this hyperbola are y=(3/4)x and y=−(3/4)x. The unit of length is omitted.
y-m-69-03.thinking.1: Building several objects that satisfy the conditions
y-m-69-03.thinking.2: Explaining why it is not determined as just one
y-m-69-03.prereq.0: Having seen a basic explanation of the form x²/a²−y²/b²=1 of a hyperbola's equation and of what an asymptote is
y-m-69-03.prereq.1: Working with fractional expressions and proportional relationships
y-m-69-03.prereq.2: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-03.s.s1.prompt: When the asymptote information alone does not determine a single hyperbola, choose all the following pieces of information that, each added on its own, would determine a single hyperbola.
y-m-69-03.s.s1.hint.0: Compare, one by one, whether the information already given and the new information carry the same content.
y-m-69-03.s.s1.hint.1: First think about whether the asymptotes determine the 'ratio of a and b' or the 'size of a and b'.
y-m-69-03.s.s1.o.a: You know the size of the angle between the two asymptotes
y-m-69-03.s.s1.r.a: The asymptotes are already given, so the angle between them is already determined. Rewriting information you already know in other words is not new information.
y-m-69-03.s.s1.o.b: The curve passes through the point (8, 3√3) (√3 is read 'root 3')
y-m-69-03.s.s1.r.b: A point on the curve can be put into the equation to determine a. You recognized that a single point also fixes the size.
y-m-69-03.s.s1.o.c: One of the two vertices is (4, 0)
y-m-69-03.s.s1.r.c: You used the fact that the position of a vertex determines a directly.
y-m-69-03.s.s1.o.d: The absolute value of the slope of the asymptotes is 3/4
y-m-69-03.s.s1.r.d: This repeats information that was already given, so there is no new information.
y-m-69-03.s.s1.o.e: The distance between the two foci is 10
y-m-69-03.s.s1.r.e: This idea tries to fix the size by using the fact that the distance between the foci is connected to a²+b².
y-m-69-03.s.s1.explain: The asymptotes determine only the ratio b/a=3/4. If a vertex is (4, 0), then a=4 and b=3. If the distance between the foci is 10, then 2c=10 gives c=5, and from a²+b²=25 and b=3a/4, a=4. Putting the point (8, 3√3) into the equation gives a=4. Restating the asymptote information is not new information.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.prompt: In the form x²/A−y²/B=1 (A=a², B=b²), make 3 different hyperbolas whose asymptotes are y=±(3/4)x. (A and B are positive; you may write decimals.)
y-m-69-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write what relationship between a and b the slope 3/4 of the asymptotes means.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.hint.1: Choose a first, adjust b to match, then square them to get A and B.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.fail.c1: A and B must both be greater than 0.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.ok.c2: Since b/a=3/4, the asymptotes are y=±(3/4)x.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Check the relationship between B and A so that b/a is 3/4. (If b/a=3/4, what is the relationship between 16B and 9A?)
y-m-69-03.s.s2.explain: With A=16, B=9; A=64, B=36; A=4, B=2.25, and so on, whenever b=3a/4 the asymptotes are all the same. Since a can be chosen freely, there are infinitely many hyperbolas.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain briefly why the asymptotes alone do not determine a single hyperbola.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the a and b of the two hyperbolas you made above side by side.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write separately what the ratio and the size each determine.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check that in your three hyperbolas the ratio of a to b is always the same, 3:4?
y-m-69-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write the difference between 'knowing only the ratio' and 'knowing the size too' in your own words?
y-m-69-03.s.s2.because.model.0: The asymptotes only tell us the ratio b/a=3/4, so a=4, b=3 works and a=8, b=6 works too. Because we can scale up the size with the same ratio, there are many hyperbolas. We need more information about the size, like a vertex or a focus.
y-m-69-03.s.s2.because.model.1: As long as the slope is the same, even if we scale a and b up by the same multiple the asymptotes stay the same, so a single hyperbola is not determined. We need information that fixes the size.

y-m-69-04.title: If the dot products are equal, are the two vectors equal too?
y-m-69-04.goal: Show by a counterexample that the claim 'if a·b=a·c then b=c' does not always hold, and say what extra information is needed to be able to say b=c.
y-m-69-04.material: Seoa said: “For a nonzero vector a and two vectors b and c, if a·b=a·c then b=c. Just as with numbers, if ab=ac and a≠0 then b=c, so we can cancel a from both sides.” Here the vectors are plane (2-dimensional) vectors, and all are written with components.
y-m-69-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the claim is true or false
y-m-69-04.thinking.2: Stating the condition under which it holds
y-m-69-04.prereq.0: Component form of plane vectors and computing the dot product with components (for a=(a₁,a₂), b=(b₁,b₂), a·b=a₁b₁+a₂b₂)
y-m-69-04.prereq.1: The fact that the dot product is 0 when two vectors are perpendicular
y-m-69-04.prereq.2: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-04.s.s1.prompt: How would you judge Seoa's claim?
y-m-69-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write what you get when you gather the equation 'a·b equals a·c' onto one side.
y-m-69-04.s.s1.hint.1: Take a to be a very simple vector like (1, 0) and look at how the dot product is computed from the components of b and c.
y-m-69-04.s.s1.r.a: You brought the cancelling rule from multiplying numbers straight over to the dot product. The dot product is a calculation that makes one number from two vectors, so the cancelling rule may be different.
y-m-69-04.s.s1.explain: Equal dot products only mean a·(b−c)=0. Even if b−c is not 0, the result is 0 whenever it is perpendicular to a, so we can build a counterexample with b≠c. Even if your first judgment was different, you can confirm it with the example you build below.
y-m-69-04.s.s2.prompt: Make two examples that go against Seoa's claim. a is not the zero vector, and you need a·b=a·c while b and c are different from each other. (a=(a₁, a₂), b=(b₁, b₂), c=(c₁, c₂))
y-m-69-04.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a, then find a vector d perpendicular to a. Think about what happens if the difference from b to c points in the direction of d.
y-m-69-04.s.s2.hint.1: In a simple case like a=(1, 0), look at which component of b the dot product a·b determines.
y-m-69-04.s.s2.explain: For example, if a=(1, 0), b=(2, 1), c=(2, 5), then a·b=2=a·c but b≠c. This is because b−c=(0, −4) is perpendicular to a, so a·(b−c)=0. The claim is false even if there is just one counterexample.
y-m-69-04.s.s3.prompt: Write how your counterexample tells you 'what you need to know to say b=c'. That is, besides a·b=a·c, write at least one more piece of information that would make b=c.
y-m-69-04.s.s3.hint.0: Gather the expression a·b−a·c as a·(b−c).
y-m-69-04.s.s3.hint.1: Draw a picture of the case where b−c is not 0 but a·(b−c)=0.
y-m-69-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain your counterexample using the equation a·(b−c)=0?
y-m-69-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you test once whether the extra information you mentioned really guarantees b=c?
y-m-69-04.s.s3.model.0: a·b=a·c means a·(b−c)=0, so if b−c is perpendicular to a, it holds even when b and c are different. So to say b=c, we need extra information that rules out the case where b−c is perpendicular to a, for example the condition d·b=d·c for another vector d that is not parallel to a.
y-m-69-04.s.s3.model.1: Equal dot products alone cannot rule out the case where b−c is perpendicular to a. If we also know that b and c both lie on the same line as a, then we can say b=c.

y-m-69-05.title: Looking at a solution that finds angle B of a triangle using vectors
y-m-69-05.topic: Dot product of plane vectors and the angle between them
y-m-69-05.goal: In a solution that finds one interior angle of a triangle using the dot product of vectors, find where the starting point of a vector was chosen wrongly, work out when that method gives the right answer, and find the correct value.
y-m-69-05.material: On the coordinate plane there are three points A(1, 1), B(5, 1) and C(6, 4). Vector AB is the vector from A to B. Seoyun found ∠B of triangle ABC (the angle formed at point B by the two sides BA and BC) using the dot product like this.
y-m-69-05.thinking.0: Locate the error in the solution
y-m-69-05.thinking.1: Consider when the error happens not to show
y-m-69-05.prereq.0: Component form of plane vectors, and the vector joining two points (AB=B−A)
y-m-69-05.prereq.1: The relationship between the dot product and the angle between vectors, cosθ=(a·b)/(|a||b|)
y-m-69-05.prereq.2: The fact that an interior angle of a triangle is the angle between the two sides going out from the vertex where they meet
y-m-69-05.prereq.3: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Seoyun's solution that you cannot trust. (It can be the line where the error first appears or a line that uses a wrong value because of it.)
y-m-69-05.s.s1.hint.1: Sketch roughly where points A, B and C are, and look at whether ∠B looks acute or obtuse.
y-m-69-05.s.s2.prompt: When you find ∠B using the dot product of AB and BC as Seoyun did, in what kind of triangle does ∠B happen to come out right?
y-m-69-05.s.s2.o.d: Always, whatever kind of triangle it is
y-m-69-05.s.s2.r.d: You thought the value found with AB and BC is the same as ∠B, so you did not see the error in the solution.
y-m-69-05.s.s2.explain: The angle between AB and BC is 180°−∠B. For this angle to equal ∠B, ∠B must be 90°. So Seoyun's method happens to be right only when ∠B is a right angle.
y-m-69-05.s.s3.prompt: Find the correct value of ∠B (to one decimal place) and explain in one or two sentences where Seoyun's solution went wrong.
y-m-69-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write the two vectors that start at B yourself.
y-m-69-05.s.s3.hint.1: Check what value you get when you add Seoyun's angle and the correct angle.
y-m-69-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you find the dot product and the value of cos again using BA and BC?
y-m-69-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check what you get when you add Seoyun's value 71.6° and your value?
y-m-69-05.s.s3.model.0: ∠B is the angle between BA=(−4, 0) and BC=(1, 3), so cos=−4/(4√10)=−1/√10, about 108.4°. Seoyun used AB, but AB points opposite to BA, so she got the angle subtracted from 180°, that is the supplement, 71.6°.
y-m-69-05.s.s3.model.1: We have to use the two vectors BA and BC going out from point B, so changing to BA=(−4, 0) makes the dot product −4 and the angle about 108°. The AB that Seoyun used is not a vector going out from B; its starting point was different.

y-m-69-06.title: Which way should you row to cross the river straight across?
y-m-69-06.topic: Sum of plane vectors and velocity
y-m-69-06.goal: Treat the flow of the river and the boat's velocity as a sum of vectors, design several velocity vectors that meet the conditions, and decide whether the same goal is possible when the flow changes.
y-m-69-06.material: The river flows steadily east at 3 m/s (north is up, east is to the right). The boat can be rowed with velocity vector v=(p, q) relative to the water (p is the east component, q is the north component, in m/s), and its top speed is 5 m/s, so p²+q²≤25. The boat's actual velocity as seen from the ground is v+(3, 0)=(p+3, q). Starting from the south bank, you want to reach the point on the north bank directly opposite. Assume that the flow of the river is constant regardless of position and time.
y-m-69-06.thinking.0: Interpreting the situation as a sum of vectors
y-m-69-06.thinking.2: Judging what is possible when the conditions change
y-m-69-06.prereq.0: Addition of plane vectors and component form
y-m-69-06.prereq.2: How velocity is written as a vector (components are positive toward the east and north)
y-m-69-06.prereq.3: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-06.s.s1.prompt: What happens if you row the boat due north at top speed (v=(0, 5))?
y-m-69-06.s.s1.hint.0: Add the boat's velocity vector and the flow vector and write the actual velocity in components.
y-m-69-06.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the east component of the actual velocity is 0 or not.
y-m-69-06.s.s1.o.a: The boat drifts east and lands to the right of the point directly opposite
y-m-69-06.s.s1.r.a: You took into account that the river pushes the boat east, so the actual velocity has an east component.
y-m-69-06.s.s1.o.b: It lands exactly at the point directly opposite
y-m-69-06.s.s1.r.b: You thought the direction the boat points is its direction of travel, leaving out the effect of the flow.
y-m-69-06.s.s1.o.c: Whatever the direction, it always goes only downstream
y-m-69-06.s.s1.r.c: You overestimated the effect of the flow and ignored the effect of the rowing speed.
y-m-69-06.s.s1.o.d: It cannot be decided without knowing the width of the river
y-m-69-06.s.s1.r.d: You mixed up the position of the landing point with the width. Whether the boat is pushed east is decided regardless of the width.
y-m-69-06.s.s1.explain: The actual velocity is (0+3, 5)=(3, 5), whose east component is not 0. So whatever the width, the boat lands east of the point directly opposite. The width only decides how far it drifts.
y-m-69-06.s.s2.prompt: Design 3 velocity vectors v=(p, q) with different values of q that let you reach the point directly opposite. Conditions: the east component of the actual velocity is 0, the boat moves north (q>0), and it does not exceed the top speed of 5 m/s.
y-m-69-06.s.s2.hint.0: Write the east component of the actual velocity in terms of p and set it equal to 0.
y-m-69-06.s.s2.hint.1: Once p is fixed, write the speed condition on q as an inequality and check the possible range.
y-m-69-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The east component of the actual velocity is 0.
y-m-69-06.s.s2.fail.c1: You must choose p so that the east component p+3 of the actual velocity is 0.
y-m-69-06.s.s2.fail.c2: q must be greater than 0 for the boat to head to the north bank.
y-m-69-06.s.s2.ok.c3: It does not exceed the top speed of 5 m/s.
y-m-69-06.s.s2.fail.c3: p²+q² is greater than 25. The boat's top speed is 5 m/s.
y-m-69-06.s.s2.explain: p must be exactly −3 to cancel the flow of 3. Then from p²+q²≤25 we get q²≤16, so 0<q≤4. If q=4, then (−3, 4) has a speed of exactly 5. The smaller q is, the more slowly the boat crosses.
y-m-69-06.s.s3.prompt: (1) Among the answers you designed, which crosses the river fastest, and why? (2) If the river flows at 6 m/s, is the same goal (arriving directly opposite) possible? Answer with reasons.
y-m-69-06.s.s3.hint.0: Let the width be d and think about d/q to see what happens to the time as the north component gets larger.
y-m-69-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write what p must be to cancel the flow, and test whether that p satisfies the speed condition p²+q²≤25.
y-m-69-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you give the 'north component' as the reason for picking the fastest answer?
y-m-69-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: For 6 m/s, did you compare how large the west component must be with the top speed?
y-m-69-06.s.s3.model.0: (−3, 4) is the fastest. The larger the north component q, the shorter the crossing time, and q can go up to 4. If the flow is 6 m/s, it is impossible. To cancel it we need 6 m/s toward the west, but the boat's top speed is 5 m/s, so the west component cannot exceed 5.
y-m-69-06.s.s3.model.1: The answer with q=4 is the fastest. To arrive directly opposite we need p+3=0, and the larger q is, the faster the crossing. At 6 m/s we cannot arrive directly opposite. To go against a flow of 6 we would need 6 toward the west, but the top speed is 5, so the boat always drifts a little.

y-m-69-07.title: What shape do the points in space that are equally far from two points make?
y-m-69-07.topic: Points equally far from two points in space coordinates
y-m-69-07.goal: Make examples to see how the plane experience (points equally far from two points form a line) changes in space, and judge the shape by checking whether the points you made lie on one line.
y-m-69-07.material: In a plane, the points equally far from two points A and B formed the perpendicular bisector (a line) of segment AB. In space there are two points A(0, 0, 0) and B(2, 4, 4), and we consider the points P(x, y, z) that satisfy PA=PB. The unit of length is omitted.
y-m-69-07.thinking.0: Testing what happens when a plane experience is moved to space
y-m-69-07.thinking.2: Working out what the examples point to
y-m-69-07.prereq.0: The distance formula between two points in space coordinates √((x₁−x₂)²+(y₁−y₂)²+(z₁−z₂)²)
y-m-69-07.prereq.1: What the perpendicular bisector of a segment is in a plane
y-m-69-07.prereq.2: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-07.s.s1.prompt: What shape do all the points P in space that satisfy PA=PB make?
y-m-69-07.s.s1.hint.0: Recall why it was a line in a plane, and count how many directions perpendicular to AB there are in space.
y-m-69-07.s.s1.hint.1: Write PA²=PB² in coordinates and check what form of equation you get after simplifying.
y-m-69-07.s.s1.o.a: Only one point (the midpoint of segment AB)
y-m-69-07.s.s1.r.a: You understood 'equal distance' in the plane as just the one midpoint. You did not test whether there are other equidistant points besides the midpoint.
y-m-69-07.s.s1.o.b: A plane perpendicular to segment AB that passes through its midpoint
y-m-69-07.s.s1.r.b: You recalled that the equal-distance condition is the space version of the perpendicular bisector.
y-m-69-07.s.s1.o.c: One line that passes through the midpoint and is perpendicular to AB
y-m-69-07.s.s1.r.c: You carried the plane experience over to space just by adding one coordinate. You have not yet tested that there is more than one perpendicular direction.
y-m-69-07.s.s1.r.d: You mixed up 'equal distance from one point' (a sphere) with 'equal distance from two points'.
y-m-69-07.s.s1.explain: Simplifying PA²=PB² gives a single linear equation x+2y+2z=9. The set of points that satisfy this equation is a plane. It is the plane through the midpoint (1, 2, 2) that is perpendicular to the direction (2, 4, 4) of AB.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different points P(x, y, z) with integer coordinates that satisfy PA=PB.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.hint.0: Start with P at the midpoint of segment AB and change one coordinate at a time while comparing the distances.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.hint.1: If you write the square of each distance, set them equal and simplify, you should see the relationship between the coordinates.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.fail.c1: x, y and z must all be integers.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.ok.c2: PA and PB are equal (their squares are equal).
y-m-69-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The squares of PA and PB are not equal. Calculate the square of the distance to each point and compare.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.explain: For example, (1, 2, 2), (3, 0, 3) and (1, 4, 0). (1, 2, 2) is the midpoint of A and B. These points all satisfy x+2y+2z=9. If you check whether the three points lie on one line, you can judge whether this set is a line or a plane.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Write how you can check whether your three points lie on one line, and write how this agrees or conflicts with the first idea that 'it is a line'.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the direction joining two points as a vector and compare it with the direction of another pair.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about why the set cannot be a line if the three points do not lie on one line.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate directly whether the directions from one point to the other two points are the same?
y-m-69-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: If your three points happened to lie on one line, did you test with more points?
y-m-69-07.s.s2.because.model.0: The vector (2,−2,1) from (1,2,2) to (3,0,3) and the vector (0,2,−2) from (1,2,2) to (1,4,0) are not parallel, so the three points are not on one line. So the set of these points cannot be a line; it is a plane.
y-m-69-07.s.s2.because.model.1: If three points are on one line, the directions from one point to the other two must be the same or opposite, but (1,2,2)→(3,0,3) is (2,−2,1) and (1,2,2)→(1,4,0) is (0,2,−2), so the directions differ. They form a plane, not a line.

y-m-69-08.title: What is the relationship between two lines parallel to a plane?
y-m-69-08.topic: Positions of a line and a plane in space
y-m-69-08.goal: Show with an example of skew lines that the claim 'two lines parallel to a plane either meet or are parallel' does not hold, and pick out the extra information that lets you say two lines lie in one plane.
y-m-69-08.material: In space, the plane α is the xy-plane (z=0). A line being parallel to α means the line is not in α and does not meet α. Sujin said: “Two lines parallel to α are both alongside the same plane α, so they always either meet or are parallel to each other.” In space, two lines that are neither parallel nor meeting are said to be in 'skew position'.
y-m-69-08.prereq.0: Positions of two lines in space (they meet, are parallel, or are skew) and what it means for a line to be parallel to a plane
y-m-69-08.prereq.1: Basics of space coordinates (x, y, z) and writing a line's direction as a vector
y-m-69-08.prereq.2: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-08.s.s1.prompt: How would you judge Sujin's statement?
y-m-69-08.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the directions of two lines must be related for the lines to be parallel.
y-m-69-08.s.s1.explain: If two lines parallel to α are at different heights and have different directions, they are in skew position. Make such an example yourself below and check it.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.prompt: Make two pairs of lines l and m that are parallel to α (z=0) and in skew position with each other. Line l passes through the point (0, 0, h₁) with direction (a, b, 0), and line m passes through the point (0, 0, h₂) with direction (c, d, 0). The heights must not be on α (0).
y-m-69-08.s.s2.hint.0: Think about how to choose the heights so that the two lines do not meet.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.hint.1: Try a few simple examples of directions (a, b) and (c, d) that are not parallel.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The heights h₁ and h₂ must not be 0, or the line would be in α.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The direction of l is not the zero vector.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The direction (a, b, 0) of l must not be the zero vector.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The direction of m is not the zero vector.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The direction (c, d, 0) of m must not be the zero vector.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.ok.c4: They do not meet because they are at different heights.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.fail.c4: If the heights are the same, both lines are in the same plane z=h, so they meet or are parallel. Try different heights.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.fail.c5: The directions are parallel. (a, b) and (c, d) must not be parallel to each other for the lines to be skew.
y-m-69-08.s.s2.explain: For example, l with height 2 and direction (1, 0, 0), and m with height 1 and direction (1, 1, 0): the two lines have different z so they do not meet, and the directions are not parallel, so they are in skew position. Both lines have constant z, so they are parallel to α.
y-m-69-08.s.s3.prompt: In addition to both lines l and m being parallel to plane α, choose all the following pieces of information that guarantee 'the two lines lie in one plane'.
y-m-69-08.s.s3.hint.0: Test one by one whether you can build a counterexample (skew lines) for each choice.
y-m-69-08.s.s3.hint.1: In the pair of skew lines you just made, change the perpendicularity or the angle and check whether they stay skew.
y-m-69-08.s.s3.o.a: l and m are perpendicular to each other (their directions are perpendicular)
y-m-69-08.s.s3.r.a: You thought perpendicular lines are in the same plane. There are also examples of lines that are perpendicular and skew.
y-m-69-08.s.s3.r.b: You used the fact that the two lines lie in the same plane parallel to α.
y-m-69-08.s.s3.o.c: The angle between l and m is 60°
y-m-69-08.s.s3.r.c: You thought knowing the size of the angle guarantees the same plane. An angle can be defined even for skew lines.
y-m-69-08.s.s3.o.d: l and m meet at one point
y-m-69-08.s.s3.r.d: You used the fact that two meeting lines determine one plane.
y-m-69-08.s.s3.o.e: l and m are parallel to each other
y-m-69-08.s.s3.r.e: You used the fact that two parallel lines determine one plane.

y-m-69-09.title: Area of the shadow of a tilted panel
y-m-69-09.goal: Sort out the information needed and not needed to find the area of the orthogonal projection of a tilted rectangle, build several heights that fit the condition, and test the guess that 'the greater the tilt, the larger the shadow' with numbers.
y-m-69-09.material: You set up a rectangular solar panel that is 2 m wide and 3 m long (area 6 m²). Of the 3 m sides, the bottom side touches the flat ground, and the top side is h m (0<h<3) above the ground. Both 2 m sides are parallel to the ground. Assume sunlight falls perpendicular to the ground, and let S be the area of the shadow (orthogonal projection) the panel makes on the ground.
y-m-69-09.thinking.0: Sorting out the information you need
y-m-69-09.thinking.1: Building several values that fit the condition
y-m-69-09.thinking.2: Testing and correcting intuition with numbers
y-m-69-09.prereq.1: The area of a rectangle, and how to find the length of the base of a right triangle from the hypotenuse and height
y-m-69-09.prereq.2: The convention that when light falls perpendicular to the ground, the shadow of a shape is called its 'orthogonal projection'
y-m-69-09.prereq.3: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-09.s.s1.prompt: You want to find S. Choose all the following pieces of information that help determine S. (Besides the sizes you already know, each counts on its own as extra information.)
y-m-69-09.s.s1.hint.0: Picture the panel seen from the side (a right triangle) and work out which value determines the remaining sides.
y-m-69-09.s.s1.hint.1: Think about which information becomes useless because of the assumption that sunlight is perpendicular to the ground.
y-m-69-09.s.s1.o.a: The compass direction the panel faces (east, west, south, north)
y-m-69-09.s.s1.r.a: You thought the direction affects the area of the shadow. Under the assumption that sunlight is perpendicular, only the position matters and the compass direction is irrelevant.
y-m-69-09.s.s1.o.b: The height h by which the top side is raised from the ground
y-m-69-09.s.s1.r.b: You used the fact that the tilt can be determined from the height and the length of the panel.
y-m-69-09.s.s1.o.c: The time of day when the sunlight falls
y-m-69-09.s.s1.r.c: You brought in the everyday experience that the shadow changes with the time. This problem assumes the sunlight is perpendicular to the ground.
y-m-69-09.s.s1.o.d: The size of the angle the panel makes with the ground
y-m-69-09.s.s1.r.d: You used the fact that this information tells the degree of tilt directly.
y-m-69-09.s.s1.o.e: The ground distance between the bottom side and the top side of the shadow
y-m-69-09.s.s1.r.e: You used the fact that the 3 m side of the shadow is exactly one side of the orthogonal projection.
y-m-69-09.s.s1.explain: The area of the orthogonal projection is determined by the 2 m side staying the same and the length to which the 3 m side is laid onto the ground. That length can be known from the height h, the angle of tilt, or the ground distance of the shadow. The compass direction and the time do not affect S under the assumption that the sunlight is perpendicular.
y-m-69-09.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different heights h for which the shadow area S is at least 4 m² and at most 5 m². (S=2×√(9−h²); you may write decimals.)
y-m-69-09.s.s2.hint.0: Put a few values of h into S=2√(9−h²) and compare whether S is between 4 and 5.
y-m-69-09.s.s2.hint.1: Compare two values to guess where the range lies, noticing how S changes as h gets larger.
y-m-69-09.s.s2.fail.c1: h must be greater than 0 and less than 3.
y-m-69-09.s.s2.fail.c2: S is less than 4. Try making h smaller.
y-m-69-09.s.s2.fail.c3: S is greater than 5. Try making h larger.
y-m-69-09.s.s2.explain: If h=1.7, S≈4.94; if h=2, S≈4.47; if h=2.2, S≈4.08. The values of h that satisfy the condition lie in a range from about 1.66 to 2.23. Be careful of calculation error for values near the boundary.
y-m-69-09.s.s3.prompt: A friend says, “The more you stand the panel up (the larger h is), the bigger the shadow gets.” Decide whether this is right, and write the reason using numbers.
y-m-69-09.s.s3.hint.0: First find what S is when h=0.
y-m-69-09.s.s3.hint.1: Find S for h=1 and h=2 and compare them.
y-m-69-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you test extreme cases such as h=0 or h close to 3?
y-m-69-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare two of your own values of h and S to check the direction?
y-m-69-09.s.s3.model.0: No. If h=0 the panel lies flat on the ground and the shadow is largest, 6 m²; if h=2 it is about 4.5 m²; and the closer h gets to 3 and the more upright the panel is, the closer the shadow gets to 0. So the larger h is, the smaller the shadow.
y-m-69-09.s.s3.model.1: Wrong. For my h=2, 2×√5≈4.47, but for h=1.7 it is about 4.94, which is larger. When h gets larger, the area of the shadow gets smaller.

y-m-69-10.title: If a line meets a parabola at one point, is it a tangent?
y-m-69-10.topic: Positions of a parabola and a line
y-m-69-10.goal: Check with a counterexample that a line meeting at one point is not always a tangent, design tangent lines yourself, and explain the conditions under which the discriminant method is used.
y-m-69-10.material: Consider the parabola y²=8x (read: y squared equals 8 x) and the line y=mx+k. The intersection points of the two figures are the solutions of the system of equations, and a line being tangent to the parabola means the two figures meet at one point and the line does not cross the curve at that point. For a circle, a line meeting it at one point was exactly a tangent. Eunchae said: “For a parabola too, if a line meets it at one point, that line is a tangent.”
y-m-69-10.thinking.0: Testing a generalization with a counterexample
y-m-69-10.thinking.1: Designing lines that fit the condition
y-m-69-10.prereq.0: The discriminant of a quadratic equation (D=b²−4ac) and the number of roots
y-m-69-10.prereq.1: How to find the intersection of the line y=mx+k and a curve using a system of equations
y-m-69-10.prereq.2: The form of the parabola y²=4px
y-m-69-10.prereq.3: The 'H1' in this task only refers to the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it does not mean the curriculum assigns this content to a particular grade. It assumes a high-school learner meeting geometry content for the first time.
y-m-69-10.s.s1.prompt: How would you judge Eunchae's statement?
y-m-69-10.s.s1.o.a: True. As with a circle, if it meets at one point it is a tangent
y-m-69-10.s.s1.r.a: You carried the property of a circle straight over to the parabola. A parabola is an open curve, so there can be situations different from a circle.
y-m-69-10.s.s2.hint.0: Substitute y=mx+k into y²=8x and rearrange as a quadratic equation in x.
y-m-69-10.s.s2.hint.1: Write the condition that the discriminant is 0 as an expression in m and k, then choose m first and fit k.
y-m-69-10.s.s2.fail.c1: If m=0 the line is parallel to the axis, so it is excluded in this design.
y-m-69-10.s.s2.fail.c2: mk is not 2, so it is not tangent. Substitute y=mx+k into y²=8x and check the condition for the discriminant to be 0.
y-m-69-10.s.s2.explain: Substituting y=mx+k into y²=8x gives m²x²+(2mk−8)x+k²=0. The condition for the discriminant D=(2mk−8)²−4m²k²=64−32mk to be 0 is mk=2. (1, 2), (2, 1) and (0.5, 4) all satisfy this condition.
y-m-69-10.s.s3.prompt: The line y=k with m=0 does not satisfy mk=2 but meets the parabola at one point. Explain why the discriminant method cannot be used as it is in this case, and whether it is a tangent or not.
y-m-69-10.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether an x² term appears in the expression you get.
y-m-69-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check directly what degree in x the expression from substituting y=k has?
y-m-69-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write in your own words that 'meets at one point' and 'is tangent' are different things?
y-m-69-10.s.s3.model.0: Substituting y=k gives k²=8x, which fixes x as one value, so it meets at one point, but the expression is linear in x, so the discriminant cannot be used. It is a line parallel to the axis of the parabola, so it is not a tangent.
y-m-69-10.s.s3.model.1: If m=0, in (0·x+k)²=8x the x² term disappears and it becomes a linear equation with only one solution. Still, it is a line parallel to the axis, so it is not tangent.
